backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Add the date of the appointment in the Appointment tab. MenoMap shows you how prepared your notes are and what would make them stronger.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most to you. Limit yourself to three or four.
- Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your healthcare professional speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and what they are not**

They are a summary of what you have logged, plus whatever you have decided to bring in from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and the patterns that appear in them are coincidence checks, not proof of the cause. Your healthcare professional may ask you questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication with its start date. In a few weeks, MenoMap will be able to show you your before-and-after logs, which will make your next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a specific moment: the day when 12 consecutive months without a period are completed, when that is not explained by something else (such as a pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it arrives, on average, in the early 50s, but it is common at any time between the mid-40s and mid-50s.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years leading up to that moment. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many of the changes associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, tend to begin here, while there are still periods. Perimenopause can last a few years or quite a lot longer, and it is different for each person.

**Postmenopause** is everything that comes after those 12 months. Some symptoms calm down over time; others can continue for years.

Menopause can also arrive earlier because of surgery in which the ovaries are removed, some cancer treatments or other health problems. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a healthcare professional.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, healthcare professionals recognise perimenopause or menopause from the history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels change from one day to the next. They are more likely to be used when the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep a faithful record of what you notice: surges, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your healthcare professional can see the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Healthcare professionals call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a racing heart or a chill afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and can be so intense that it wakes you or soaks your sheets.

They are among the most frequent changes around menopause. Some people have a few, mild ones; others have many a day, which disrupt work and sleep. In some they disappear within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many people notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy bedding. This varies a lot from person to person, and that is why logging your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes.** Redness and sweating can also be due to thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or general malaise, mention it to a healthcare professional.

**How to describe them well.** Useful details for the appointment:
- How many you have per day and at night, roughly
- How intense they are and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to happen beforehand
- What you have tried and whether anything changed

MenoMap's Surge button and retrospective logging exist to capture exactly this without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical measures. Which suit you is something to discuss with a healthcare professional.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces part of the oestrogen that the body produces less of around menopause. The main guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. People who still have their uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen along with the oestrogen to protect the inner lining of the uterus.

**The benefits and risks depend on each person:** age, the time since the period stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and the type and route of treatment. That is why it is a decision to be made with a healthcare professional who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions that are commonly asked:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me? Why or why not?
- Which type and which form would be most suitable for me, and why?
- What benefits could I expect, and how soon?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not being treated?
- What should I watch out for, and when should we review it?

**If you already take it,** log it in MenoMap (You → Medication). MenoMap will show you your surges before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so that you have something concrete to discuss at the review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everybody, and some people simply prefer other routes. There are several.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence that they reduce hot flashes. Among them are certain medications originally developed for other conditions and a more recent class designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a healthcare professional can help you weigh them up.

**Psychological therapies and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and that it improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that many people find useful:**
- Layers of clothing you can take off quickly
- A fan on the desk and beside the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Spotting and easing your personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this)
- Regular physical activity and a stable sleep routine

**Supplements and plant-based products.** For many of them the evidence is contradictory or limited, quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell your healthcare professional or your pharmacist everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own logs before and during a change, something easier to assess than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. We tend to remember the most recent days or the worst ones. A simple log fills that gap.

**What a diary gives your healthcare professional:**
- How often symptoms appear and how intense they are, not just that they appear
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point to compare against if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only helps if you keep it up. MenoMap is designed around a one-tap Surge button and a four-question review of the day, so it takes seconds, not a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of logs usually give a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Appointment tab helps you choose questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
When you have gone 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a healthcare professional**, even if it has happened only once, and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time, the cause turns out not to be serious. For example, it is common for the lining of the vagina or the uterus to become thinner. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat if caught early. That is why public health recommendations say to get it checked rather than wait.

**If you take hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns can be expected, depending on the type you take. Bleeding that is not expected with your treatment, that is heavier than usual or that appears at a time it should not also needs to be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your healthcare professional or your health centre and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can store it for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding has occurred. It will remind you to get it checked and will include it in your notes for the appointment.

backTranslations.529:
Sleeping badly is one of the most frequent complaints in midlife, and it rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too hot or too damp to fall back asleep.

**Other frequent factors:**
- Having to urinate at night
- Anxiety or a racing mind
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but usually fragments the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or your partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea (worth mentioning, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers you can take off; a fixed time to get up, and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many healthcare professionals can point you towards it.

**What to log.** For one or two weeks, note your sleep score, night surges, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's review of the day and surge log do it in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show you sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app next to your night sweats, as context and not as an explanation.

**When to mention it.** Talk to a healthcare professional if sleeping badly affects your safety (for example, when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or choking at night.

verdict: Pass. All 64 blind back-translations match the English source in meaning. Post-menopausal bleeding is consistently 'should be checked by a healthcare professional', with 'even once, even light' (130) and 'even if only once / spotting / light pink or brown' (479) intact. Emergency and urgency wording (278 'seek care now', 388, 401, 403, 717, 718) keeps its qualifiers and urgency. Medication and hormone therapy strings keep 'never suggests starting, stopping or changing' and 'decision with a healthcare professional'. Coincidence-check-not-proof language is preserved everywhere, and there is no added advice or diagnostic tone. No fixes needed.
